## Operating conventions

# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Work decide

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. Build the queue: requirements waiting for approval, designs marked proposed, items at stage 11 waiting for result approval, Open Questions rows where the owner decides, and memory proposals (records saved as `needs-review` because the owner did not answer "Save to memory?"). The command lists each decision once. Its "Agent to-do" lines are the agent's own steps, not decisions waiting on the owner: count and show only the decisions. A delivery offer, as an agent to-do or as an open question, belongs to `work-delegate`, the only skill that makes or records it: open it after the owner's other decisions.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. The owner gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision. If two could match, ask which one, naming both. A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" is not such an answer ("What counts as an answer").
3. Otherwise take the decisions one at a time, the one blocking the most work first. For each: what is being decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue; a bare question is not enough. One decision per message, asked in the reply text.
4. A requirements approval: save his words as a history note first, so no later session asks him again. Then check the Agreed goal and the open questions. The goal still holds the template text: write the goal he was shown with the approval question, then record the approval. A requirement still has an open question linked: say which one, open `work-requirements` for it, and record the approval, without asking him again, once it is answered.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner'\''s words: <quote>' --effect 'Requirements approval to record.'`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --text '<goal he was shown>'`
5. Record each answer where it belongs. Approvals (for requirements, first set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and put who approved it and when in its Decision record, as `work-requirements` step 8 does; after it, a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design` unless the owner agreed to skip the design, and a skip is said in the final reply). The approve command marks the Open Questions rows that asked for that approval Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; read that line, and do not mark those rows again by hand. An Open Questions answer: rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and status Answered (the delivery offer row: open `work-delegate`, which records it).
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --set-file <file>`
   Then, for an approval or an answer: `waiting_on` set to `agent` when the agent continues (the approve command sets it to `none` by itself), unless another question for him on that item is still open; then one history note in the owner's words, with an `--effect` that says what the answer changes (a requirements approval has its note from step 4).
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner'\''s words: <quote>' --effect '<what the answer changes>'`
6. A memory proposal: show its one line and whether you recommend keeping it. The agent does not rely on it until he approves it. Yes: approve it, and it becomes a current memory. No: reject it (the proposal is deleted), and never propose the same fact again under other words.
   `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory reject <key>`
7. A decision for the whole project: add a `DECISIONS.md` row and save it with `publish-docs`. Run the command inside the worktree `publish-docs` opens, then let it commit (and push, when the project has a remote).
   `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>`
8. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
9. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. When an answer changed an item's next step, update the current focus (`../../references/conventions.md`, "The current focus"). When the queue is empty, say so and offer to continue unblocked items with `work-on`. End the reply with the next decision's question, or the exact words that continue.

## What counts as an answer

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in the history note. The lifecycle command prints the full approval rules:
  `toolkit work lifecycle`
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), or silence is not an answer. Ask again in one line.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
- A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" answers only a question asked earlier in this conversation. When none was asked, or the waiting question is not a yes-or-no question, show the decision with its choices and your recommendation, and record nothing.
- Set `waiting_on` to `agent` when the agent can continue, to `none` when nothing waits, or keep `owner` when another owner question is still open on that item.

## After a result approval

The item continues with `work-finish` (pull request, deployment, requirements baseline, Done). Open it when the owner wants it shipped now.

## Project-wide decisions

- A decision for the whole project goes in `DECISIONS.md`, not in memory and not in one item. Examples: "use Postgres everywhere", and a standing merge instruction ("agents may merge a pull request after an independent check finds no blocking issue").
- A decision that replaces an older one names it with `--replaces D-<n>`:
  `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner> --replaces D-<n>`
- A decision about one item stays in that item: its Recent History, the answered Open Questions row, and Notes > Decisions and context when the next session needs the context.
- `DECISIONS.md` is append-only. Never rewrite or remove a row; a changed decision is a new row that names the one it replaces.

## Tracker notes

- GitHub Issues or Jira: the `toolkit work` commands exit with code 3. Build the queue from the waiting-on-owner and stage 11 labels that `../../references/trackers/github.md` or `../../references/trackers/jira.md` names, and record answers as `../../references/trackers.md` says. Remove the waiting-on-owner label after each approval or last answer, as above.

# Work requirements

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). Interview and writing rules: this skill's `references/writing-requirements.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does; none exists, create it. Use discovery while the goal is being worked out, refinement once requirements are being written. Requirements already approved and no change asked: stop and open the skill the lifecycle's "Continue with" column names.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
2. Before asking anything, read the item (Starting request, Agreed goal, `R-xx`, Open Questions) and look up what the project already knows, so no question repeats an answer.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
3. Restate the goal in one sentence ("So the goal is X?"). Write the Agreed goal after a yes, and always before asking for approval in step 8.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --text '<goal>'`
4. Ask one question at a time, most basic first, each with a recommended answer and a short reason. Push back when an answer works against the goal.
5. Write each answer into the item before the next question: `R-xx` blocks (Status Refining, required behavior, boundaries, acceptance check, decision record) and the Acceptance list, with each section's fill-in guide comment left out once it holds real content. Anything unanswered becomes an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with who must answer; the item waits on the owner while one of his is open, and goes back to the agent when he answers the last one. Build ideas go under Notes > Solution options and considerations, never into requirements. A fact the owner cannot answer: brief a `researcher` agent.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Active requirements" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
6. A change to an approved requirement: edit the `R-xx`, keep the old wording in its decision record, set it back to Refining, move the item to refinement, and say what the change affects when the item is past stage 03.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
7. Spec check, before asking for approval and whenever the owner says "check the spec": brief the `requirements-analyst` agent with the requirements text. Fix what it finds or turn it into questions. Change nothing without a yes.
8. With the Agreed goal written (the CLI refuses an approval while it holds the template text), show the goal and a short summary and ask one line, in the reply text: "Do you approve these requirements?" and set the item waiting on the owner. Yes: quote his words in one note first, set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and put who approved it and when in its Decision record, record the approval (the command adds its own history row), and hand the item back to the agent unless another question for him is still open. Then a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design`, unless the owner agreed to skip the design; say a skip in the final reply, not a progress line. Not yet: it stays waiting on him.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner'\''s words: <quote>' --effect 'Requirements approved.'`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Active requirements" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
9. Lead with "Not saved" on a failed write. Check the item, update the current focus when its next step changed (`../../references/conventions.md`, "The current focus"), then hand back to `work-on` unless the owner stops. End the reply with the one question for the owner, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `requirements-analyst`: the spec check in step 7. Paste in the Starting request, Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, the Acceptance list, and the open questions.
- `researcher`: one per fact the owner cannot answer (a platform limit, what the existing build does).
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Spec check findings

The analyst reports: missing pieces; places not explicit end to end; wording a builder could misread; build details inside requirements; drift from the Agreed goal; research or history in the wrong place. For each finding, propose a fix in plain words. The owner approves, edits, or dismisses each one. A dismissed finding stays dismissed for this item in this session. Clean spec: say so in one line and move on.

## Notes

- "Grill me" means a deep interview: keep asking, one question at a time, until every branch that could change the result is covered. End with "What have we not touched that could change this?"
- The owner thinks out loud; let him. Save settled answers as they come; do not wait for the interview to end.
- Brainstorming methods from other plugins may run inside this skill. The answers still land in the work item.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Edit the issue body's Requirements section as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

name: work-on
description: 'Starts, resumes, or logs a work item and builds it. Use whenever the owner asks to build, add, fix, or change something, names an item id to resume, says "keep going", or wants a bug or idea logged ("put it in the backlog"). Not for requirement edits (work-requirements) or handovers (work-delegate).'
---

# Work on

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` (saving, section edits, history, branches) and `references/trackers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. A bare "ok", "yes", or "looks good" is not "keep going": when it is the owner's whole message and this chat asked him nothing, start no work and ask what he wants. No session briefing in this conversation: run the command below. Exit code 4 (no `.toolkit.json`): open `project-setup` and stop. When the briefing or a `toolkit work` command lists changes found in the tracker (a moved or renamed folder, a new parent, a missing item), tell the owner each one in one line in the reply, not only in a progress line, before other work. Use the CLI's own words for what changed; do not guess at a cause it does not name.
   `toolkit brief`
2. Find the item: the id the owner named, or a title in the list that matches the request. Two possible matches: ask one question naming both. No match: it is new. When `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` names the item, read its phase there too.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work list`
3. Size a new request. Setup is not a work item: never create one for setup steps. Owner setup steps go in the reply; only a step doctor checks (trust the hooks in Codex, `ntn login`) also goes in the current focus under "Waiting on the owner", marked as a setup step, and leaves it once doctor stops reporting it. "Start a new session" goes in the reply only. "New work", "track", "work item", or "done properly" always makes an item. When the owner names a deliverable but not what it should say or do ("write a short project brief"), create the item, add the content question as `Q-01` with the item waiting on him, and ask it in the reply before building anything; never fill the content in yourself. A quick edit (one sitting, no choice for the owner, no behavior recorded in `requirements/`, nothing bound for production): do it and report it, with no item. "Later", "backlog", "park that": check the list for a duplicate, create the item, write the owner's words unchanged into Starting request, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop. Anything else: create it the same way, titled in the owner's words (say the title in one line), and continue.
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Starting request" --text '<his exact words>'`
4. An item that shows `delivery: not-offered` once it reaches stage 03 or later, an item the briefing lists with the agent to-do "Make the agent-led delivery offer", or an owner who hands the goal over in his own words ("you drive"): open `work-delegate` first. It is the only skill that makes the offer, and it records owner-led at once for a small item. Never ask the offer here. When it asks the offer, wait for his answer before building. Quick questions and small edits get no offer.
5. Route by where the item stands, using the item and the "Continue with" column of the lifecycle. Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load`, or the owner answered the questions that set them, or asked for it done properly: `work-requirements`, which shows them to him for approval. A change the owner asks for to a requirement (`R-xx`), at any stage: `work-requirements`. More than one reasonable way to build it and no approved design: `solution-design`. A `build` item going to planning without a design: say so in the final reply, not a progress line ("One way to build this: <approach>. I'll build it that way; say 'design first' to stop me."), and put the reason in a history note. An item that changes committed files goes through stage 07 (its own worktree), never onto the default branch. Too big for one build: `work-organize`. Stages 09 to 11: `work-check`. Stages 12 to 14: `work-finish`. `waiting_on: owner`: ask that one question first (`work-decide`) and keep working on anything it does not block. Say the route in one line ("WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements; opening work-requirements."). Never ask the owner which stage it is in.
   `toolkit work lifecycle`
6. Plan (stage 06): Roadmap phases `P1`, `P2` and tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) from the design's "Build and verification plan", in the table and checkbox format in this skill's own `references/planning.md` (the `references/` folder beside this `SKILL.md`; read it first): each task's `**Work:**`, `**Deliverable:**`, `**Done when:**`, and `**Depends on:**` on its own line. Tracking setup (stage 07) only when needed: the item's worktree `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on branch `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, with the item's own id prefix in lower case (`wi-007-...` for WI-007, `tv2-007-...` for TV2-007; the show command in step 2 prints the branch and folder to use); in a Salesforce project, the item's folder in `delivery/deployment/` through `sf-component-tracker`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 06-implementation-plan`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>`
7. Build (stage 08) on the item's own branch and worktree, never on the default branch. Commit with files staged by name and a plain message with no AI credit: no `Co-Authored-By` line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line. In Codex, `git worktree add`, `git add`, and `git commit` need the owner's approval and escalated permissions (`sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason), because the sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only: say in one line what each does before Codex asks. Refused without asking: show him the exact command, ask him to approve it or run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting on the owner. Never work around it (the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, "Branches and worktrees"). With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per independent task, one writer per path. Tests go with each task. Tick a task only with evidence. A task whose "Done when" names the owner is a question for him (step 8). Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` on each metadata change; production data only through `sf-data-change`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 08-build`
8. When the owner is needed: add an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with "owner" as who decides, set the item waiting on the owner, keep working on tasks that do not depend on the answer, and tell him in one line. After his last answer, set it back to the agent (`../../references/conventions.md`, "Waiting on the owner").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | <affects> | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Last task done: open `work-check`. This skill never records approvals, Done, merges, or deploys.
10. Before stopping with work unfinished: Overview (Current position, Next action) and Notes > Resume here are current, one history note says what changed, validation is clean, and the current focus names the item and its real next step (`../../references/conventions.md`, "The current focus"). End the reply with the one question for the owner, or the exact words that continue ("Say 'keep going' and I'll build P1.").
   `toolkit work history <id> --note '<what changed>'`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `builder`: one per independent build task, only when `work-delegate` recorded a team or the owner agreed to one. The main agent merges each builder's branch into the item's branch, then ticks the task.
- `researcher`: one per unknown found while planning or building.
- `acceptance-checker`: a plan check after step 6, before the build, when the plan has several builders, parallel tasks, or a shared environment. Paste in the requirements, the design's "Build and verification plan", the Roadmap, and the Tasks, and ask for a plan check.
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Sizing a request

- **Quick edit, no item:** one sitting, no decision for the owner, and it does not change behavior recorded in `requirements/`. Examples: fix a typo, rename a variable, answer a question. Report what changed in one line.
- **Log only:** the owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or "log a bug". Create the item at `01-discovery`, fill Starting request with his exact words, and stop. Do not start the work.
- **Work item:** everything else. A request that grows past a quick edit while you work on it becomes an item then, with the owner's words as the Starting request.
- Types: pick the closest from the lifecycle's type list. `build` and `data-load` need approved requirements before stage 03 is passed; the CLI refuses otherwise. A change to what the product does, to Salesforce metadata (`force-app/`), or to anything bound for production is `build` (data changes are `data-load`), never `task`, even when it looks small.

## Routing notes

- The lifecycle's "Continue with" column is the default. The item's real state decides: for example, a `task` type item with no open choices can skip requirements approval and go straight to planning, with the reason in a history note.
- Stages may be skipped, repeated, or revisited. Record a short reason when a move is not obvious.
- A worktree whose branch names an item (`claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, for example `claude/wi-007-csv-export`) belongs to that item. The briefing says so. Work on that item there.
- Several items at once: recommend what can proceed independently, what depends on another outcome, and which decision would unblock the most work. See this skill's own `references/planning.md`.
- `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` holds the project's phases (`P01`) and deliverable-sized work units, each naming its work item ID; item detail stays in the tracker. A new item that is one of those units gets its ID written into the unit, saved with `publish-docs`. An item's own phases (`P1`) are a different thing and live in its Roadmap section.

## Never

- Never record an approval, Done, or a cancel here. Those belong to `work-requirements`, `solution-design`, `work-check`, `work-decide`, and `work-finish`.
- Never merge, deploy, or write production data.
- Never create a second tracker or a local copy of items kept in Notion, GitHub, or Jira.

name: memory-save
description: 'Saves, corrects, or forgets one lasting fact in the project''s memory, or sends it to the record where it belongs. Use when the owner says "remember this", "from now on", "forget that", or "remind me" with no time given, corrects the agent, or a hook says a save is due.'
---

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion). Text: one-line values (`--description`, `--source`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)` and drop that text. A record body, the focus, or the glossary: in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--body-file -` or `--set-file -`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), never through a file; in Codex give it in single quotes (`--body '<text>'`, `--text '<text>'`), or write a file with the file edit tool in a new folder made with `mktemp -d`, run the `toolkit` command alone with that file, and delete the file and the folder right after. Never write the file and run the command in one shell command, and never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate. The save command checks too: when memory already has a record with the same key or a very similar description or text, it saves nothing, exits with code 2, and lists those records. Read each one with the second command below, which prints its `version` field. The same fact: save that record's type and slug again with `--expect <version>`, which updates it (the first 12 characters of the version are enough; for a record with the same key, the command's own fix line already gives them). A newer fact that replaces it: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. A different fact: say why in one line and save again with `--allow-similar`. Never add `--allow-similar` without reading the listed records.
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
   `toolkit memory get <key> --json`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. An unanswered "Save to memory?" (his next message does not answer it, or the session is ending) is not dropped: save it as a proposal (`--proposal`, never with an approver). A proposal is not a fact: search leaves it out, the agent does not rely on it, and the decision list shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it through `work-decide`.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body with the model's bold labels, each starting its own paragraph: `**Remember:**`, `**Why:**` (the owner's reason in his words, or "Not stated by the owner."; never a reason you inferred), `**How to apply:**`, `**Evidence and limits:**` (the source and an absolute date), `**Related memories:**` (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), `**Authoritative records:**`. Never write them as `## headings`. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again, with `--expect <version>` (the `version` field of the step 2 read), updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. A better name or a type that matches the content: rename it; links to it are repaired. The first form is for the owner's approval (his words or his yes); the second for a routine save in `trusted` mode; the third for an unanswered proposal; the fourth updates a record read in step 2. `<file>` is `-` in Claude Code.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>'`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --proposal`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus with its version, change it, write the whole text back. The model's format: the `# Current focus` title line, a "Last updated" line (date, source, who), and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status; keep the title and the date line (the CLI adds them when missing, but without the source and who). Drop a setup step under "Waiting on the owner" once doctor no longer reports it. On a new project remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus --json`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." (a proposal: "Saved as a proposal for your yes or no: <title>."). A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses. End the reply with the question still waiting for him, if there is one, or those exact words.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Changing the approval mode

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.
- Switch to trusted, or back to onboarding:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase had no save this turn. Save it, or tell the owner in one line why it belongs elsewhere and where it went.

## Proposals and declined saves

- A proposal saved in step 3 waits for the owner's yes or no; `work-decide` asks him. His answer in this chat also settles it: yes approves it (a current record with him as the approver), no rejects it (the proposal is deleted).
  `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
  `toolkit memory reject <key>`
- When the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it (a saved proposal: reject it). Do not put the rejected fact in the current focus, the glossary, or another record, and never propose it again under other words. If his words give a general rule about what to save, save only that rule, as a `feedback` record.
- Several independent things can be grouped into one save. Never run two saves against the same record or the index at once.

## Backend notes

- Built-in `.memory/`: never edit the files by hand; the CLI writes them and rebuilds `.memory/MEMORY.md`. The folder opens as an Obsidian vault. When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.
- Undo a retire:
  `toolkit memory restore <key>`
